{"notes": "My seat is 2s10s slope, so I filter this panel down to the four drivers that actually bear on front-vs-long balance: balance_sheet, curve_slope, term_premium, and labor_tightness. Everything else (financial conditions, risk appetite, sector breadth, positioning, vol regime) is level/risk-sentiment noise that doesn't differentiate the two ends of the curve, so I set those aside entirely regardless of their conviction.

Balance_sheet is the standout: fresh (formed this meeting), conviction 0.60, calling the balance sheet UP — i.e. QT is easing or reserves are being added back. A growing/less-shrinking balance sheet is disinflationary for term premium and tends to cap long-end yields more than front-end (which is anchored by policy rate), a flattening-to-bull-steepening ambiguous signal on its own, but combined with the direct curve_slope read of "flat" (0.40 conviction, fresh) and term_premium "flat" (0.35, fresh), I don't see enough to call an aggressive steepener or flattener from the term premium/duration-supply side.

Labor_tightness is flat but stale (23 days old) — I discount its weight further; if it were moving toward tighter labor that would argue for front-end pressure and flattening, but at flat with staleness, I give it near-zero incremental read.

Net: the direct curve_slope call says flat, term_premium confirms flat, and balance_sheet up is a mild disinflationary/duration-supply-reducing force that nudges long yields down relatively more than front-end, giving a very slight flattening bias — front end anchored by rates, long end capped by balance sheet expansion. This is a marginal call, not a strong one.</notes>

My mandate is the 2s10s slope, so I strip out the equity/vol/positioning analysts (financial_conditions, positioning, risk_appetite, sector_breadth, vol_regime) since they speak to risk sentiment and level, not the front-vs-long differential, and I have no clean mapping from them to curve shape. Balance_sheet down (0.75, fresh, meaning the balance sheet is shrinking/QT continuing) tends to add long-end duration supply into private hands, which historically steepens the curve as term premium/supply concerns build at the back end — this actually cuts against the term_premium read, creating a genuine front-vs-long tension. Labor_tightness up (0.40, stale by 23 days) implies a tighter labor market, which supports front-end yields staying anchored/higher on Fed-hold expectations — a flattening force via the front end holding up while long end is capped by term premium compression. Curve_slope itself reports flat with only 0.35 conviction — weak, near-neutral.

Weighing these: labor_tightness is stale, which weakens its front-end pull. Balance_sheet's steepening implication (via supply) is highest-conviction but is a longer, month-end structural force that often plays out with lags and can be offset by weak term premium and demand-side flight to duration if risk-off (which the discounted risk pods collectively suggest, though I set them aside for slope purposes). Given term_premium and curve_slope's own direct call both lean flatter, and labor_tightness (stale) reinforces flatter front-end anchoring, I lean modestly toward flattening, but keep conviction low given the balance_sheet counter-pull and weak signal-to-noise in curve_slope's own read.

But term_premium analyst, also fresh and second-highest conviction, says term premium is compressing — a genuine long-end flattening force. Direct curve_slope call agrees with term_premium's flattening implication. Two of three long-end-relevant reads (curve_slope direct, term_premium) point to flattening; only balance_sheet points to steepening. I weight toward mild flattening, tempered by balance_sheet's high conviction pulling against it — net a modest, low-conviction flattener.

The others in this panel (financial_conditions, inflation, inflation_expectations, labor_tightness, positioning, risk_appetite, sector_breadth, vol_regime) are largely equity/cross-asset or level-oriented signals without a clear, disambiguated front-vs-long transmission channel supplied here, so I treat them as not directly informative on slope and set them aside — though labor_tightness is nominally in my remit as one of the four core drivers I'm asked to weigh.

Direct evidence: curve_slope itself reports "up" (steepening) at moderate conviction (0.45), freshly formed. balance_sheet reports "down" (shrinking) at high conviction (0.78), freshly formed — a shrinking balance sheet (QT continuing/accelerating) tends to pressure term premium and the long end more than the front end (which is anchored by policy rate expectations), which is a steepening force on the curve. term_premium itself is reported flat (0.35, weak), which somewhat tempers the balance-sheet-driven steepening story but doesn't reverse it given the more confident and fresher balance_sheet read plus the direct curve_slope call agreeing on direction.

labor_tightness is flat and stale (22 days), giving essentially no signal and, being a front-end-relevant driver, a flat/stale read here does not push toward flattening — it just adds no information, so I don't lean on it to offset the steepening case.

Putting this together: two of my three most relevant, freshest reads (curve_slope directly, balance_sheet indirectly via long-end pressure) point toward modest steepening, while term_premium is neutral. I'll take a modest-conviction steepener view, not a high-conviction one given term_premium's neutrality and the moderate size of the direct curve_slope conviction.
